It was shaped by choices about what counts as relevant, who can publish, how platforms make money, how users are guided, and how machines should read data. Those older choices still sit underneath current search engines, knowledge graphs, large language models, and agentic AI systems. The need for the paper comes from a practical risk: if researchers treat current AI as a sudden break from the past, they may miss the repeated tensions that the Web has already exposed, including reliability, governance, scale, accountability, and social impact.
323.wh: The hard part is that Web history is not a clean timeline where one invention simply replaces another. Search ranking, user experience design, platform engagement, Semantic Web ideas, knowledge graphs, and language models overlap and inherit each other's assumptions. A choice that first looked technical, such as ranking pages by usefulness, later became social because ranking controls visibility. A choice that first looked open, such as letting many people publish and link, later became a governance problem because openness also spreads low-quality or harmful information. Large language models make this even harder because they use the Web in several roles at once: as infrastructure, as an archive of training material, as an evaluation setting, and as a place where generated outputs affect people. The central tension is separating what is genuinely new from what is a recurring Web problem wearing new technical clothing.
323.naive: A smart beginner might handle this track by listing milestones: early search, ranking, user experience, platforms, the Semantic Web, knowledge graphs, then large language models and agents. That list would be accurate but shallow. It would make history sound like a museum shelf instead of an explanation of current design pressure. Another beginner move would be to ask whether each era was good or bad. That also fails, because the abstract emphasizes tradeoffs rather than simple verdicts. Relevance can improve search while weakening reliability. Openness can enable creativity while making governance harder. Scale can make systems useful while making accountability harder. The track needs a way to compare recurring tensions across eras, not just name the eras.
323.ap: The core idea is to use history as an analytical instrument. Instead of treating older Web systems as background, the track asks how historical decisions, institutional incentives, and socio-technical shifts continue to constrain today's systems. It traces a connected path from information retrieval and ranking, through user experience and platform dynamics, into the Semantic Web's attempt to make data understandable by machines, and then into present language models and agentic AI. The central move is comparison across time: look at a current problem, then ask which older Web choice helped create it, which tension it repeats, and which part is actually new. That turns history into a practical design tool. It helps researchers ask better questions about responsible and durable future systems because it shows that current choices will also become future infrastructure.
323.mech: The mechanism begins with a set of historical Web layers. The first layer is retrieval and ranking: the Web became useful only when systems could choose a small set of useful pages from a huge collection. The second layer is user experience, engagement, and platform dynamics: once ranking controlled attention, platforms began shaping how people moved, clicked, stayed, and interacted. The third layer is the Semantic Web and knowledge graphs: researchers tried to make web data less like loose text and more like connected facts that machines could inspect and reason over. The fourth layer is current language models and agents: these systems absorb Web material, answer questions over it, act through it, and are judged inside it. The track then compares tensions across these layers. Relevance is compared with reliability: does the system retrieve what looks useful or what can be trusted? Openness is compared with governance: who may publish, reuse, train on, or control web material? Scale is compared with accountability: can a system serve many people while still explaining and correcting its consequences? What comes out is not a single score or model. It is a structured map of how past design choices continue to shape present AI research.
323.math: The mathematical ideas are mostly implicit, but the abstract names the historical systems that forced them into the Web. Ranking is the act of turning many candidate pages, posts, facts, or answers into an order when only a few can receive attention. Its useful compression is also its danger: one order can hide disagreement between relevance, reliability, freshness, authority, and social value. Knowledge graphs use network reasoning. A graph is a map of things and relationships; evidence can travel along links when connected facts constrain each other. That fits the Semantic Web vision because machine-understandable data requires more than words in a document. It needs typed relations that say what connects to what. Large language models add statistical learning from examples: they reuse patterns found across huge Web archives, which works when repeated text patterns reflect useful knowledge and fails when the archive contains errors, bias, missing voices, or outdated assumptions. The repeated mathematical tradeoff is compression versus accountability. Ranking compresses many signals into an order. Graphs compress facts into links. Language models compress Web-scale text into reusable behavior. Each compression saves time and enables scale, but each can also hide why a result appeared.
323.dots: This track connects directly to recurring conference ideas rather than sitting outside them. Information retrieval and ranking papers ask how to choose useful evidence from an overwhelming pile, which is the same old Web pressure named in the abstract. Knowledge-graph and Semantic Web papers ask how to turn scattered facts into linked structure so machines can follow relationships instead of relying only on loose text. Large-language-model and agentic-AI papers ask what happens when models use the Web as training data, tool environment, and evaluation arena. The neighboring themes in the repo around retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge graphs, recommendation, platform dynamics, misinformation, trust, fairness, and governance all share the track's deeper question: when a technical system sorts, summarizes, or acts on Web material, whose values and past choices are being carried forward? The track's contribution is to make those inheritance lines visible.
323.ww: The historical lens works because Web systems are cumulative. A current AI system rarely starts from a blank world. It receives data from old pages, interfaces shaped by old platform incentives, search habits shaped by ranking systems, and knowledge resources shaped by earlier attempts to describe the world for machines. When the track compares eras, it helps distinguish surface novelty from structural repetition. A language model may be new in its fluent generation, but the reliability question resembles earlier search questions: did the system surface something merely plausible, or something trustworthy? An AI agent may be new in its ability to act, but the governance question resembles older platform questions: who sets the rules for action at scale? This works better than a milestone list because it follows pressures. If relevance, openness, scale, and social impact keep reappearing, then future systems can be judged by how they handle those pressures, not only by how impressive their capabilities look.
323.po: The payoff is a clearer way to reason about Web research and AI innovation. The track gives researchers a connected story that links early retrieval and ranking to user experience, platform incentives, Semantic Web ambitions, knowledge graphs, and today's language-model and agent systems. That story helps identify which problems are genuinely new, which are cyclical, and which remain unresolved. Practically, it can sharpen design and evaluation questions: not just whether a system works, but whether it is reliable, governable, accountable at scale, and socially responsible. The abstract's claimed result is intellectual orientation, not a new benchmark or deployed tool.
323.limits: The main limit is that the abstract describes a track program, talks, and a panel rather than a single empirical study. It does not provide datasets, experimental results, exact historical cases, or a detailed method for deciding when a current problem is new versus recurring. Its claims depend on the program actually making the promised connections across retrieval, ranking, user experience, platform dynamics, Semantic Web ideas, knowledge graphs, large language models, and agents. The approach also assumes that historical comparison can guide technical judgment without flattening differences between eras. That is plausible, but the abstract does not prove it. The output should therefore be read as a framing lens grounded in the track description, not as evidence that any specific policy or system design will succeed.

324.bp: Cloud quantum computing creates a strange trust problem. A user sends a quantum circuit to a remote quantum processor because the hardware is too expensive or specialized to own. The machine runs the circuit, but real quantum hardware is noisy, so the raw answer often needs quantum error mitigation: extra processing that tries to cancel some of the machine's mistakes after the run. The catch is that useful mitigation normally needs to see the circuit structure and understand the service provider's noise behavior. Both sides may treat those details as proprietary. The user's circuit can reveal research or business value, while the provider's noise model can reveal how its hardware behaves. Blind-QEM serves this setting. It tries to let a provider clean up noisy quantum results while proving it followed the agreed policy, without forcing either side to expose the private object it wants protected.
324.wh: The central difficulty is that usefulness and secrecy pull against each other. If the provider sees the whole circuit topology, it can choose a stronger mitigation procedure because it knows which operations were connected and how errors may spread. But revealing that topology may leak the user's intellectual property. If the user sees the provider's full noise model, the user can better judge whether the corrected result deserves trust, but the provider may consider that model commercially sensitive. A simple locked-room approach also fails: if nobody sees enough detail, nobody can tell whether the mitigation was applied to the right circuit, whether the policy was respected, or whether the returned answer came from the promised quantum processor execution. The abstract's phrase privacy-utility dilemma names this exact tension. The hard part is not only hiding information. It is hiding information while still leaving enough evidence for verification, correction, and mutual accountability.
324.naive: A smart beginner would make one side trust the other. The user could reveal the circuit to the service provider, let the provider perform the best available error mitigation, and rely on contracts or reputation to protect secrecy. That fails when the circuit itself is valuable. Another beginner answer is to hide the circuit completely and ask the provider to return only raw aggregate measurement results. That protects the topology better, but it removes the information normally needed for effective quantum error mitigation. A third attempt is to ask for a signed execution receipt, but a receipt alone does not prove that the mitigation followed the promised policy or that the returned result is cryptographically tied to the committed circuit.
324.ap: Blind-QEM's core idea is to split the job into three linked acts: commit, prove, and mitigate. The user commits to the circuit so there is a fixed private object that later results must match, but the provider does not learn the circuit topology. The quantum processor supplies signed execution logs, which act like tamper-resistant receipts saying what execution event the hardware claims occurred. Zero-knowledge proofs then let one party prove a rule was followed without revealing the private details behind the rule. In everyday terms, the proof says, the hidden circuit and the reported handling satisfy the agreed checks, while keeping the hidden circuit hidden. Once that verification layer is in place, the provider can do global incoherent noise cancellation and readout mitigation using verified aggregate statistics instead of raw circuit visibility. The central move is not secrecy alone, but verified outsourced correction under secrecy.
324.mech: The mechanism begins with a private quantum circuit from the user and a cloud service provider that will run and mitigate it. First, the circuit is committed. A commitment is like sealing a document in a way that fixes its contents: later claims can be checked against the same sealed object, but the contents are not openly readable. Second, the quantum processing unit runs the job and produces signed execution logs. These QPU-signed logs are receipts from the hardware side, anchoring the later answer to an actual execution event rather than to an unsupported claim. Third, Blind-QEM uses a receipt-based binding mechanism to cryptographically connect the committed circuit, the execution logs, and the returned results. Binding matters because a corrected answer is only meaningful if it belongs to the circuit the user actually submitted. Fourth, zero-knowledge proofs verify policy compliance. The proof does not reveal the circuit topology; it demonstrates that the hidden objects and the provider's actions satisfy the required relation. Fifth, the provider performs error mitigation from verified aggregate statistics. The abstract names two mitigation operations: global incoherent noise cancellation, which tries to subtract a broad pattern of hardware noise, and readout mitigation, which corrects mistakes made when the quantum state is measured. The output is a mitigated result tied to the committed circuit and protected on both sides.
324.math: The mathematical ideas are commitment, proof without disclosure, binding, and statistical correction. A commitment is a locked promise: it fixes a secret value now so it cannot be changed later, while still keeping it hidden until or unless opening is allowed. Zero-knowledge proof is the verification idea: prove that a statement is true without revealing the private witness that makes it true. Here the witness includes hidden circuit information and possibly other private compliance details. Binding is the rule that prevents swapping one hidden object for another after seeing results. The signed QPU log adds authentication, meaning the verifier can check that the receipt came from the claimed hardware source. The mitigation side uses aggregate statistics. Instead of exposing every private detail, the system counts repeated measurement outcomes and uses those counts to estimate and reduce error patterns. Noise cancellation is a correction problem: estimate the unwanted distortion and subtract or compensate for it. Readout mitigation focuses on measurement mistakes, where the hardware may report one outcome when another was produced. The tradeoff is verification versus exposure: the math must reveal enough structure to prove the correction is legitimate, but not enough to reconstruct the circuit topology or the provider's noise model.
324.dots: This paper belongs to the repo's Privacy, Federated and Security family because it asks what useful signal can cross a boundary without exposing the private object behind it. It sits near federated recommendation papers such as FeDecider, where clients share shaped model information instead of raw user histories, and near security papers such as SPCA and IntelGuard, where trust fails at the boundary between components. The common pressure is controlled sharing: one party needs help from another party, but the information that would make help easiest is also sensitive. Blind-QEM also connects to the information concept in the current data. It uses aggregate statistics as the allowed information channel, while circuit topology and provider noise details remain restricted. Compared with ordinary privacy-preserving learning, the object here is unusual: not a user record or text sample, but a quantum circuit and the correction process around noisy quantum hardware.
324.ww: Blind-QEM should improve over the naive approach because it separates knowing from checking. A service provider may not need to know the full circuit topology if the protocol can still prove that the hidden circuit, execution receipt, mitigation procedure, and final result fit together correctly. Zero-knowledge proofs are useful precisely when the important question is whether a rule was followed, not whether the verifier gets to inspect every private detail. The signed execution logs add a second anchor: they reduce the chance that a result is presented without being tied to an actual quantum processor run. The receipt-based binding mechanism then makes substitution harder, because the result must stay linked to the committed circuit. Aggregate statistics give the provider a narrow channel for utility. Repeated outcome counts can carry enough information to support global incoherent noise cancellation and readout mitigation, while leaving out the topology details that would reveal the user's design. The method works when the hidden proof relation captures the right policy checks and when aggregate statistics preserve the noise signal needed for mitigation.
324.po: The payoff is outsourced quantum error mitigation with mutual protection. The user can seek better answers from noisy cloud quantum hardware without handing over circuit topology. The service provider can perform correction without exposing its noise model in full. The abstract specifically says Blind-QEM enables global incoherent noise cancellation and readout mitigation using only verified aggregate statistics. It also cryptographically links results to committed circuits and verifies policy compliance through zero-knowledge proofs and QPU-signed execution logs. In practical terms, it turns cloud quantum correction from a pure trust arrangement into a verifiable privacy-preserving workflow.
324.limits: The abstract does not report experiments, runtime cost, proof size, hardware overhead, or the exact policy language being proved. The approach assumes QPU-signed execution logs are available and trustworthy, and that the signing infrastructure itself is not compromised. It also assumes aggregate statistics are sufficient for the named mitigation tasks; some stronger mitigation methods may need circuit details the protocol withholds. Zero-knowledge proofs verify a formal statement, so the guarantee is only as good as the statement and implementation. The abstract does not prove protection against side channels, malicious hardware, colluding parties, weak commitments, or future attacks that infer topology from repeated aggregate outputs.

325.bp: The paper starts from a very practical web-platform problem: a conference has many papers and many reviewers, and every paper must be assigned to someone. These assignments are chores, because reading and evaluating a paper consumes time. But the same paper is not equally painful for every reviewer. If a reviewer bid on a paper, the model treats that assignment as carrying no cost for that reviewer, because the reviewer has already signaled interest or fit. If the reviewer did not bid on it, the paper carries its inherent cost, such as the effort implied by its length. The platform therefore wants two things at once. It wants low total burden across all reviewers, and it wants no reviewer to be stuck with a bundle that looks plainly worse than someone else's. The paper studies this as fair resource allocation, where the resource being allocated is unwanted work rather than a prize.
325.wh: The difficulty is that fairness and efficiency pull against each other. If the platform only minimizes total effort, it might give every bid-on paper to interested reviewers and dump the remaining costly papers on a few people. The total cost could look good while the workload feels unacceptable. If the platform only equalizes the number of papers, it ignores the fact that one long or unwanted paper can be more burdensome than several easy ones. The model is also sharply two-valued for each reviewer-paper pair: the cost is either zero or the full inherent cost. That makes local reasoning dangerous, because an assignment that is free for one reviewer may be expensive for another. The paper must satisfy EFX, meaning envy should disappear after removing any single chore from the envied bundle, and MMS, meaning each reviewer should receive a burden no worse than a reasonable fair-share benchmark. It must do this while keeping total cost near the best possible.
325.naive: A smart beginner might first sort papers by cost and spread the expensive ones evenly, or assign each paper to someone who bid on it whenever possible. Each rule handles only one part of the problem. Spreading expensive papers evenly ignores that an expensive paper may be free for a bidder and costly for everyone else. Greedily honoring bids can lower total cost, but it may leave a small set of unwanted papers to be concentrated on unlucky reviewers. Equal paper counts fail for the same reason: counts do not measure burden. The hard part is choosing a whole assignment where each reviewer's bundle is fair when judged by cost, while the platform still avoids unnecessary total effort.
325.ap: The paper's central move is to treat the review assignment as a chore-allocation problem with a very specific cost shape. Each paper has one inherent cost, and each reviewer either pays zero for it because they bid on it or pays that inherent cost because they did not. This restricted additive cost model keeps the problem structured enough for a provable algorithm, while still matching the review-platform story. The algorithm is designed to output an allocation that satisfies two fairness tests at the same time: EFX and MMS. It also controls efficiency by proving that the total social cost, meaning the sum of all reviewers' incurred costs, is at most twice the best possible social cost. The abstract also says this factor of two is optimal for the guarantee being sought, so the result is not merely an arbitrary bound but the best approximation ratio possible under the stated model.
325.mech: The input is a set of reviewers, a set of papers, an inherent cost for each paper, and bid information saying which reviewer-paper pairs should have zero cost. From this, the system can compute what every possible assignment would cost each reviewer: zero if the reviewer bid on that paper, otherwise the paper's inherent cost. The algorithm then has to choose a partition of the papers, one bundle per reviewer. For each candidate bundle, costs add up across papers, because the model is additive: a reviewer's burden is the sum of the costs of the papers assigned to that reviewer. The mechanism must keep three checks visible while it builds or searches for an allocation. First, it checks EFX: if one reviewer compares their own burden with another reviewer's bundle after any single chore is removed from that other bundle, the comparison should not reveal unacceptable envy. Second, it checks MMS: each reviewer should do at least as well as their maximin-share benchmark, the level they could guarantee by dividing the chores into bundles while expecting to receive the worst bundle. Third, it tracks social cost, the total incurred effort across everyone. The output is one assignment of all papers to reviewers that meets EFX and MMS and whose total cost is within a factor of two of the minimum possible total cost.
325.math: The main mathematical object is an allocation table. Rows are reviewers, columns are papers, and each cell has a cost: either zero or the paper's inherent cost. Choosing an allocation means selecting exactly one reviewer for each paper, then adding the selected cell costs reviewer by reviewer and in total. This is matching and allocation math: the question is not whether one paper fits one reviewer in isolation, but which whole arrangement of pairings works together. The fairness math supplies two tests. MMS, maximin share, imagines a reviewer splitting all chores into bundles and then receiving the worst bundle; it is a way to define a fair burden without assuming everyone has identical costs. EFX, envy-free up to any chore, asks whether another person's bundle would still look better after removing a single item, so it prevents fairness from depending on one unusually costly chore. The efficiency math is approximation: because perfect minimum social cost may conflict with fairness, the algorithm proves a ratio against the best possible social cost. A 2-approximation means the total burden is no more than twice that best cost, and the abstract says no better ratio is possible here. The tradeoff is fairness versus total effort.
325.dots: This paper sits in the conference's fair resource allocation thread, but it also connects to matching and efficiency. Like recommendation or expert-routing papers, it asks who should be paired with what under limits; unlike ordinary recommendation, the assigned object is work that must be covered, not an item a user may simply ignore. It also connects to optimization, because the system must define what counts as costly and then search for an arrangement that reduces that cost while obeying fairness rules. The local data also contains another WWW 2026 chore-allocation paper, All-but-one MMS Allocation for Chores, which studies what happens when exact MMS-style fairness cannot be fully achieved and one relaxes the guarantee. This paper takes a different path: under restricted additive costs, it aims to achieve EFX and MMS together, then measures the efficiency price through a provably optimal factor-two social-cost bound. The shared deeper problem is how a platform can allocate unavoidable burdens without sacrificing trust.
325.ww: The reason the approach can work is that the restricted cost structure gives the algorithm useful order. In a completely arbitrary chore problem, every reviewer might experience every paper with unrelated costs, making fairness comparisons messy. Here, each paper has one inherent cost, and bids only switch that cost off for particular reviewers. That means the algorithm can reason about assignments using a clear map of free versus costly pairings. Bids help efficiency because assigning a paper to a bidder avoids effort that another reviewer would incur. But bids alone are not enough, so the fairness conditions stop the algorithm from concentrating the remaining costs on a few reviewers. MMS anchors each person's burden to a fair-share baseline, while EFX checks the more immediate human complaint: whether someone else's bundle would still look preferable after discounting any one chore. The approximation result explains the price of satisfying those fairness rules. The paper does not claim to always reach the absolute lowest total cost; it claims the unavoidable extra burden can be bounded, and that this bound is the best possible for this setting.
325.po: The payoff is a stronger assignment rule for platforms that must distribute unwanted tasks. In the motivating review-platform example, it gives a way to use reviewer bids to reduce wasted effort without letting efficiency alone decide who gets the hard leftover papers. The stated result buys simultaneous EFX and MMS fairness, plus a total-cost guarantee within twice the optimum, with that factor shown to be optimal. The abstract also adds a practical note: if polynomial running time is required, slightly weaker fairness guarantees are available. So the contribution is both conceptual and algorithmic: it identifies a structured chore model and shows exactly what combination of fairness, efficiency, and computational demands can be achieved.
325.limits: The claims depend on the restricted additive cost model being a good description of the real platform. In practice, a bid may not mean zero effort; it may mean interest, expertise, or strategic behavior. Paper cost may also involve more than length, and reviewer capacity constraints are not described in the abstract. The abstract states the existence of an algorithm, fairness guarantees, a factor-two social-cost approximation, optimality of that ratio, and weaker polynomial-time guarantees, but it does not give implementation details, empirical review-assignment results, or evidence about strategic bidding. The result should therefore be read as a mathematical guarantee for the stated model, not proof that every real conference assignment process will be fair in practice.

326.bp: Online shopping used to be designed around a person looking at a page, noticing product order, reading prices and reviews, and deciding what to buy. This paper asks what changes when that chooser is an autonomous AI agent acting for the shopper. The practical system is not just a recommender inside a store; it is a buyer-side agent that can read webpages or use platform interfaces, compare listings, and transact. That makes its behavior commercially important. If many shoppers delegate buying, then sellers will compete for the agent's attention rather than only the human's eye. Platforms will also need to know whether their page layout, sponsored labels, endorsements, ratings, and review counts steer agents in predictable or unfair ways. The paper builds ACES to study that question before real agentic commerce becomes too large to inspect cleanly.
326.wh: The hard part is that an AI agent's purchase is the end of many hidden judgments. A product may be chosen because it is cheaper, because it has better ratings, because it appears first, because it has an endorsement, or because a particular model reads a page in a particular order. In a live marketplace these factors are tangled together: popular products often have more reviews, higher placement, more endorsements, and different prices. It is also unsafe to assume that all agents share one notion of the best position on a page. The abstract says all models favored the top row, yet different models preferred different columns, which means a supposedly neutral layout may advantage products differently depending on the agent model. The central tension is measurement versus entanglement: to understand agent buying, the researchers need to separate layout effects, listing attributes, and model-specific habits.
326.naive: A smart beginner would send several AI agents to a real shopping site, record what they buy, and compare the final choices. That would show differences, but it would not explain them. If one model buys a higher-priced item, was it responding to ratings, review volume, position, endorsement text, or a sponsored label? Another beginner would inspect a single model and generalize from it. The abstract shows why that fails: modal choices can differ across models, and sensitivity to position, price, ratings, and reviews varies sharply. A third naive approach is to treat the top rank as a universal advantage. The paper finds that top-row bias is shared, but column preference is not universal.
326.ap: The core idea is to replace the messy real marketplace with a fully programmable mock marketplace where the researchers can move one piece at a time. ACES pairs a platform-agnostic agent with a sandbox store. Platform-agnostic means the agent is not built only for one merchant's website; it can interact through webpages or interfaces in a more general way. The researchers first observe aggregate choices: which products each model tends to pick when facing the same marketplace. Then they run randomized experiments. Randomized means product positions and listing attributes are deliberately varied so that a change in choice can be tied to the changed feature rather than to some unrelated product difference. This turns agentic e-commerce from anecdote into controlled measurement: what agents buy, how concentrated their choices become, and which layout or listing signals steer each model.
326.mech: The mechanism starts with a mock marketplace whose products and presentation can be programmed. The input is a set of product listings with visible attributes such as position on the page, price, ratings, review counts, endorsements, and sponsored tags. An AI agent is then asked to act for a consumer in that marketplace. It may parse the webpage or interact through an interface, evaluate the listings, and choose a product to buy. The first output is an aggregate choice pattern: across repeated runs or conditions, which product becomes the modal choice for each model, and whether choices concentrate on only a few products. The second stage changes from observation to experiment. The researchers randomize product positions and listing attributes, then compare how the agent's purchase changes when one signal is moved or relabeled. Position experiments ask whether row and column placement pull choices even when product substance is otherwise controlled. Attribute experiments ask whether sponsored tags reduce appeal, endorsements increase appeal, and price, ratings, and reviews affect choices in the expected direction. The key comparison is not only product A versus product B. It is also model A versus model B under the same marketplace. The output is a map of model-dependent buying behavior: shared top-row effects, different column effects, penalties for sponsored labels, rewards for endorsements, and varying sensitivity to price and review evidence.
326.math: The main mathematical idea is controlled comparison under uncertainty. Controlled comparison means changing one visible cause at a time, or randomizing changes so accidental product differences do not masquerade as causes. Here the uncertain thing is why the agent chose a product. A final purchase is only one observed action, but many signals could have pushed it. Randomized experiments give a cleaner language for this problem: if product position is assigned by chance, then repeated differences in buying after that assignment are evidence that position itself matters. Ranking is another core idea. A marketplace page turns many products into a visible order, and order saves attention by deciding what gets seen first. The danger is that this compression can create bias: the page location may become a reason to buy, separate from product quality. Probability appears in aggregate choices and modal choices. A modal choice is the most common outcome, useful when agents do not always make the same decision. The tradeoff is realism versus control. A sandbox may not capture all real shopping pressure, but it lets the researchers measure price, ratings, reviews, sponsored labels, endorsements, and layout separately. The paper also uses model comparison as a measurement object: the same marketplace is passed through different AI systems to expose where behavior is shared and where it depends on the model.
326.dots: This paper sits across three repo neighborhoods. In advertising and e-commerce, it studies how commercial attention is allocated when listings, labels, endorsements, and prices compete for a buyer's choice. In recommender systems, it reverses the usual viewpoint: instead of asking how a platform ranks products for users, it asks how an agent acting for the user ranks the platform's products. In LLM agents and tool use, it treats the model as an actor that reads, compares, and transacts, not merely as a text generator. It also connects to recurring conference ideas of ranking, probability, causal measurement, and marketplace design. The closest sibling pressure is agentic shopping evaluation, such as benchmarks for product curation and production shopping agents. ACES adds a sharper measurement question: when agents buy, which parts of the marketplace surface are steering them, and are those steering effects model-dependent enough to change competition?
326.ww: ACES works better than the naive real-site audit because it separates causes that real commerce naturally mixes together. If a live product is first on the page and also cheaper, a purchase tells little about whether the agent liked the price or the placement. In a programmable marketplace, the same product can be moved, tagged, endorsed, or repriced under controlled conditions. That lets the researchers turn a vague behavioral question into many small comparisons. The approach also works because it treats model identity as part of the experiment. If every model favored the top row, that suggests a shared page-reading or attention pattern. If different models prefer different columns, that shows the effect is not a universal property of e-commerce layout. Penalizing sponsored tags and rewarding endorsements are interpretable because the labels are visible listing attributes, not hidden product traits. The method should reveal practical failure modes early: seller strategies that exploit agent habits, platform layouts that unintentionally favor certain products, and regulatory issues around concentration if agents repeatedly choose only a few listings.
326.po: The payoff is a measurement system and an initial behavioral map for agentic e-commerce. ACES gives researchers, platforms, sellers, and regulators a way to ask what AI agents buy and why under controlled marketplace changes. The reported findings are concrete: modal choices differ across models, agents can concentrate on a few products, all models favor the top row, column effects vary by model, sponsored tags are penalized, endorsements are rewarded, and sensitivity to price, ratings, and reviews differs sharply. That buys earlier visibility into competition and platform-design risks before autonomous shopping agents become routine commercial intermediaries.
326.limits: The claims depend on the ACES sandbox and the models tested. A programmable mock marketplace gives control, but it may omit real-world frictions such as user budgets, brand loyalty, shipping, returns, fraud, inventory changes, and strategic seller adaptation. The abstract does not say which models were tested, how many shopping tasks were run, or whether actual consumers would approve the agents' purchases. It reports current drivers of choices, but agent behavior may change as models, prompts, tools, and marketplace interfaces change. The results show steering and model dependence; they do not prove consumer harm, illegal discrimination, or long-run market concentration by themselves.

327.bp: Imagine a large machine learning model trained on graph data (like user-item networks for recommendations). You want to adapt it to a new domain (like a different set of items) without forgetting what it learned before. But you need to do this for many domains in sequence—one after another—without the model collapsing into chaos. How do you continuously adapt a graph model across many new domains without catastrophic forgetting?
327.wh: Standard fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting: after adapting to domain 2, the model forgets domain 1. Adding a regularizer (a penalty for changing too much) helps but hurts performance. Cross-domain adaptation is harder because domains have different graph structures. When you add adapters (small specialized models) for each domain, they can interfere with each other. And measuring what the model has learned across domains is hard because graph models don't learn explicit, comparable representations.
327.ap: G-CORMoL uses something called orthogonal mixture-of-experts with LoRA adapters. Each domain gets its own small adapter (LoRA), but these adapters are mathematically orthogonal—perpendicular in a high-dimensional space, so one adapter's changes don't interfere with another's. A routing network learns to blend the adapters dynamically, pulling in expertise from multiple past domains when needed. A contrastive objective (a training trick borrowed from self-supervised learning) pushes different adapters to specialize on different aspects of the problem.
327.ww: This works because orthogonality is a mathematical way to prevent interference: if you try to rotate vector A orthogonally and then apply changes to vector B (also orthogonal), changing B doesn't affect A. A router that learns a global policy means the model can reuse past adapters intelligently, enabling positive transfer. Contrastive specialization ensures each adapter learns something distinct.
327.po: The model can now adapt across many domains in sequence without forgetting prior domains and without degrading performance. It even gets better over time as it accumulates knowledge from past domains. This matters for recommendation systems and other applications where you want one model to serve multiple distinct user groups or item categories simultaneously.

328.bp: In social networks and graphs, communities are clusters of tightly-connected people. A common task is to identify the community a given user belongs to, starting only from knowing the user. If you know Alice, can you find her community without exploring the entire network? This is called local community detection and is useful for real-time recommendation and personalization.
328.wh: The standard approach starts with a seed node (Alice) and expands outward, adding neighboring nodes until you've traced out the full community. But this expansion is prone to accumulated errors: each step depends on the previous step, so mistakes compound. If the seed node is on the boundary (at the edge of a community rather than the core), the expansion can easily drift into a neighboring community. Semi-supervised methods use a few labeled examples to help, but weak supervision makes it hard to correct accumulated errors.
328.ap: SLFM (Semi-Supervised Local community detection based on hyperbolic Flow Matching) reframes the problem as generative: instead of expanding outward, think of it as transporting probability distributions. Start with a distribution centered on the seed node, then use a learned vector field to transform that distribution into one centered on the full community. The system has three pieces: a Seed Selector that uses hyperbolic geometry to validate and improve the seed node, a Flow Transporter that learns how to smoothly morph distributions, and a Community Expander that uses the transported distribution as guidance.
328.ww: This works because treating community detection as transport of probability distributions lets you smooth out accumulated errors—you're not making discrete expansion decisions but learning a continuous path. Hyperbolic geometry is good at modeling hierarchical structures (central, core nodes are near the origin; peripheral nodes are far out), so the seed selector can validate whether your starting point is central or boundary. The flow transporter is learned from weak labels and naturally handles partial information.
328.po: The system is robust to bad seed nodes and weak supervision, finding communities even when you start from a boundary user. This matters for real-time recommendation systems that need to quickly identify user communities for personalization without expensive expansion.

329.bp: Online platforms host billions of pieces of content—memes, images with text, videos, news articles—that can spread misinformation, hate speech, or propaganda. Moderating this at scale is impossible by hand, so platforms use AI. But today's moderation tools work with text or images separately. What if you could use multiple types of signals together—text, images, even temporal patterns across platforms—to understand and moderate multimodal content better?
329.wh: A meme is a single image with text overlaid; hatespeech requires understanding both together. A video showing something suspicious might only become obviously problematic when combined with the audio narration. And a narrative that's okay in isolation becomes dangerous when amplified by coordinated sharing across platforms. Most AI systems are built for single modalities (text only, image only) and miss these cross-modal nuances.
329.ap: MM4SG 2026 (the fourth workshop on Multimedia Content Analysis for Social Good) convened researchers from NLP, computer vision, machine learning, computational social science, and ethics to tackle multimodal moderation. A major theme was how to use large vision-language models (VLMs)—models that reason about both images and text together—and agentic systems (AI systems that act autonomously) to scale moderation. The workshop emphasized interpretability and ethical grounding, not just accuracy.
329.ww: This works because treating content as inherently multimodal captures the full story. A hateful image gains its power from the text overlay; a false claim gains traction from the authority signaled by a video. By reasoning over multiple modalities, systems can catch context that single-modality tools miss. Agentic systems can make decisions autonomously but with human oversight.
329.po: The workshop aimed to advance the state of the art in detecting and moderating synthetic content, memes, and cross-platform narratives. This matters because platforms serve billions of people, and moderation at that scale requires AI that understands context, not just pattern matching—and because decisions about speech have real social impact.
